pairs.rationale: Both letter openings identify the named writer as a servant in relation to Jesus Christ and address recipients. Jude additionally identifies himself as James’s brother; the comparison does not establish which other person named James is intended from the greeting alone.

Both greetings address recipients with mercy and peace. Jude asks that mercy, peace and love be multiplied; Timothy’s greeting names grace, mercy and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. The lists and grammatical forms remain distinct.

Jude urges contending for the faith delivered once for all to the saints. Philippians urges standing together and striving for the faith of the gospel. The common faith-directed struggle is explicit, while Jude’s delivered-once-for-all qualification remains his own.

Jude describes people slipping in unnoticed and denying the only Master and Lord Jesus Christ. Peter warns of secretly introduced destructive factions and denial of the Master who bought them. The target does not supply every detail of Jude’s grace-perversion charge.

Paul recalls the ancestors’ passage through the sea, identifies the spiritual rock as Christ, and says God was not pleased with most, who were strewn over the wilderness. Jude explicitly names Jesus saving from Egypt before destroying unbelievers; that named agency is retained.

Both describe sinning or disobedient angels kept in chains of gloom for judgment. Jude specifies abandoning their proper dwelling and everlasting chains; Peter names Tartarus and chains of gloom. Neither set of additional details is inserted into the other account.

Genesis narrates the Lord raining sulphur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah and overthrowing their cities and surroundings. Jude recalls these cities as an example of punishment, adding sexual conduct and eternal-fire language not all stated in the retained narrative.

Both accusations join defiled flesh or defiling desire, rejection of dominion or despised lordship, and slander of glorious ones or beings. Jude adds dreaming; Peter adds recklessness and self-will. The three corresponding charges preserve the distinct wording and unnamed referents.

pairs.relationship: the Lord’s rebuke of the devil
pairs.rationale: Zechariah’s separate scene contains the Lord’s rebuke addressed to the slanderer. Jude places the same appeal to the Lord’s rebuke in Michael’s dispute with the devil over Moses’s body. Slanderer/devil wording and the different actors and disputed matter remain distinct.

Both compare the opponents with unreasoning or irrational animals and connect slandering what they do not understand with corruption or destruction. Peter adds capture and repeated destruction language; Jude distinguishes what they slander from what they understand instinctively.

Genesis narrates Cain rising against Abel his brother and killing him. This supplies the fratricidal episode behind Jude’s named example of Cain’s way. Jude’s accusation against the present intruders is not a claim that they literally repeated that same killing.

Peter names Balaam’s love of wrongdoing’s wages, directly corresponding to Jude’s Balaam-error-for-pay accusation. Peter adds the patronymic Bosor and leaving the straight way. Those details are not made part of Jude’s shorter wording or silently normalized.

Numbers narrates the ground opening, the rebels descending alive and fire consuming the incense-offering men. These judgments supply the narrative background to Jude’s named Korah rebellion, without collapsing the different participants or modes of death into one action.

Peter calls people feasting with the readers spots and blemishes while describing their deceptions and indulgence. Jude calls them reefs at love feasts and adds self-shepherding, waterless clouds and fruitless trees. Reefs is retained rather than substituted with Peter’s blemishes.

Peter describes waterless springs and storm-driven mists for whom darkness’s gloom is kept. Jude describes shame-foaming waves and wandering stars with gloom kept forever. The reserved-gloom correspondence preserves the different images and Jude’s explicit duration.

pairs.relationship: the Lord with His holy company
pairs.rationale: Jude’s quoted prophecy says the Lord came with His holy myriads; Thessalonians speaks of the Lord Jesus’s coming with all His saints. The past-form came, the coming formulation and myriads/saints wording remain distinct. This does not identify Thessalonians as the source of Enoch’s words.

Jude’s judgment oracle includes conviction for harsh things ungodly sinners spoke against Him. Jesus says people must account for idle words on judgment day and speaks of condemnation by words. The target supports speech’s accountability without reproducing Jude’s entire oracle or naming Enoch.

Peter joins inflated words of emptiness with desire-driven enticement. Jude joins walking according to desires with boastful speech and flattery for advantage. The related combination of desire and manipulative speech retains the distinct adjectives and descriptions of those affected.

Both urge remembrance of words spoken beforehand and connect the instruction with the apostles of Jesus Christ. Peter also explicitly names the holy prophets and the Lord’s commandment; that wider list is not silently inserted into Jude’s sentence.

Jude recalls mockers in the last time walking according to ungodly desires. Peter predicts scoffers with scoffing in the last days following their own desires. The close pattern preserves mockers/scoffers, the time expressions and Jude’s additional ungodly qualification.

pairs.relationship: the merely natural and the Spirit
pairs.rationale: Paul says the natural person does not receive the things of God’s Spirit. Jude labels the divisive people unspiritual and without the Spirit. The contrast concerns their relation to the Spirit, not proof that the two passages identify the same people or use identical predicates.

Jude directs building on most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit. Ephesians directs prayer and petition at every time in the Spirit with perseverance for the saints. The prayer instruction corresponds; each passage’s surrounding commands retain their own scope.

pairs.relationship: mercy and the hope of eternal life
pairs.rationale: Titus connects saving mercy, renewal and the Spirit poured out through Jesus Christ with heirs according to hope of eternal life. Jude directs awaiting Jesus Christ’s mercy leading to eternal life while keeping in God’s love. Their agency, tense and surrounding instructions remain distinct.

Peter cries for the Lord to save him, and Jesus immediately grasps him before asking why he doubted. This concrete help amid doubt can be read beside Jude’s command of mercy for doubting people, without claiming the command narrates Peter’s water-walking event.

Zechariah combines a brand rescued from fire with filthy clothing removed from the high priest. Jude combines snatching others from fire with hatred of a tunic stained by flesh. The paired images correspond without equating the persons, clothing or narrated and exhortatory settings.

Paul prays that the God of peace sanctify the readers and keep them whole and blameless at Jesus Christ’s coming. Jude praises the One able to guard from stumbling and present them blameless before His glory. The prayer and praise retain their different formulations.

pairs.relationship: glory to God through Jesus Christ
pairs.rationale: Both ascribe glory to God through Jesus Christ and extend the praise across ages. Jude says the only God our Savior and adds majesty, might, authority and before-all-time wording; Romans says the only wise God. The additional titles and time expressions remain distinct.
